blocks.text: Cracking is a chemical process in which large hydrocarbon molecules (typically from naphtha or heavy oils) are broken down by heat into smaller, more useful molecules such as alkenes. It is needed because ethene and propene, which are small molecules, are the major raw materials for plastics and artificial rubber. The two main methods are thermal cracking and catalytic cracking.

Thermal cracking uses very high temperatures (usually 450-750 C) and high pressure to break carbon-carbon bonds. No catalyst is used, so the process needs a high energy input. It usually gives a high percentage of alkenes, which matters for the plastics industry. For example, decane can be cracked to octane and ethene: C10H22 -> C8H18 + C2H4.

Catalytic cracking is more efficient and is used more in modern refineries. A catalyst, usually zeolites (aluminosilicates) or silica-alumina, greatly lowers the activation energy, so the process works at lower temperatures (about 500 C) and pressures, saving energy and giving better control over the products. For example, the heavy fraction naphtha is cracked over a catalyst to give a blend of short-chain alkenes such as ethene (C2H4) and propene (C3H6).

blocks.alt: Top: thermal cracking drawn as carbon skeletons; a ten-carbon zigzag chain (decane, C10H22) is cut by a red dashed line and, on heating, gives an eight-carbon chain (octane, C8H18) plus a double bond (ethene, C2H4); conditions 450-750 C, high pressure, no catalyst. Bottom: catalytic cracking: naphtha over a catalyst gives ethene (C2H4) and propene (C3H6); zeolites or silica-alumina, about 500 C.
blocks.caption: Thermal and catalytic cracking (original diagram for topic 31.6.1).
blocks.long_description: Cracking breaks one long chain into shorter pieces. Since there are not enough hydrogen atoms for every piece to be saturated, at least one product is an alkene such as ethene.

blocks.text: Reforming is a refining process that rearranges the molecular structure of hydrocarbons. Unlike cracking, where molecules are broken down, reforming changes straight-chain alkanes into branched or cyclic (aromatic) structures. Its main purpose is to improve fuel quality by turning low-octane straight chains into high-octane branched or aromatic fuels, which prevents engine knocking.

items: Isomerisation (forming branched hydrocarbons): straight-chain hydrocarbons become branched isomers with higher octane numbers, e.g. C6H14 -> iso-C6H14 (n-hexane to iso-hexane).
Cyclisation (forming cyclic hydrocarbons): straight chains form rings, e.g. C6H14 -> C6H12 + H2 (hexane to cyclohexane).

Aromatisation (the book calls it dehydrocoupling): hydrogen is removed to give aromatic compounds such as benzene, toluene and xylene (BTX), the building blocks of plastics, dyes and synthetic fibres. Hexane, a straight six-carbon chain, becomes a stable aromatic ring and releases hydrogen as a valuable by-product: C6H14 -> C6H6 + 4H2 (Pt catalyst, heat).

blocks.title: Hexane, not cyclohexane
blocks.text: The book labels the equation C6H14 -> C6H6 + 4H2 as '(cyclohexane to benzene)'. C6H14 is hexane, and the equation is balanced for hexane. Starting from cyclohexane the equation would be C6H12 -> C6H6 + 3H2. The process from hexane is usually called dehydrocyclisation or aromatisation.

blocks.alt: Three rows. 1, isomerisation: a six-carbon zigzag (hexane) gives a five-carbon chain with a one-carbon branch (2-methylpentane), C6H14 -> C6H14. 2, cyclisation: hexane gives a plain hexagon (cyclohexane) plus H2, C6H14 -> C6H12 + H2. 3, aromatisation over a Pt catalyst: hexane gives a hexagon with an inner circle (benzene) plus 4H2, C6H14 -> C6H6 + 4H2.
blocks.caption: The three reforming reactions of hexane (original diagram for topic 31.6.1).
blocks.long_description: All three start from the same straight chain. Isomerisation keeps the formula but adds a branch; cyclisation closes a ring and loses H2; aromatisation also forms the benzene ring and releases four molecules of H2.

blocks.prompt: Why is catalytic cracking more commonly used in modern refineries?
blocks.explanation: It is more efficient: the catalyst lowers the activation energy, so it runs at lower temperature (about 500 C) and pressure, saving energy and giving better control over the products.

blocks.prompt: If more alkenes such as ethene and propene are wanted from diesel or kerosene, which cracking method should be preferred and why?
blocks.explanation: Thermal cracking, because the book states that it normally gives a high percentage of alkenes.

blocks.prompt: During reforming, hexane is converted into benzene and hydrogen. Why is hydrogen a valuable by-product?
blocks.explanation: Hydrogen is a clean fuel with a very high specific energy (about 120 MJ/kg) and is a useful raw material, for example for making ammonia.

items: Cracking: large molecules to smaller ones and alkenes.
Thermal: 450-750 C, no catalyst; catalytic: zeolites, about 500 C.
